item.title: 55.6% of cross-border workers believe Swiss residents earn more
item.description: 55,6% consider their salary to be lower 48,4% report a decrease in purchasing power 73% say they are satisfied with their compensation 1.542 workers.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 55,6% considers their salary lower - 48,4% reports a decrease in purchasing power - 73% states that they are satisfied with their pay - 1.542 workers in the survey presented in Varese
## Key facts - Study → Cisl and OCST - Research → BiblioLavoro with the local Cisl branches - Sample → 1.542 workers - Presentation → Saturday in Varese - Wage comparison → 55,6% consider it unfavorable - Purchasing power → 48,4% say it has decreased - Satisfaction → 73% - Private car → 73,2% of respondents
According to the research, 55,6% of the workers surveyed believe they receive a lower salary than a resident of Switzerland performing similar duties. The study was conducted by the BiblioLavoro center with the Cisl branches of the Lakes, Sondrio and Eastern Piedmont, and with OCST, together with the Italian trade union Cisl. Presented on Saturday in Varese, the survey involved 1.542 workers who cross the border daily to go to work.
The result does not amount to a generalized negative assessment of pay. 73% of respondents say they are satisfied with their remuneration. The share reporting a disadvantage compared with a Swiss resident differs from the satisfied share by 17,4 percentage points, calculated from the figures in the same survey. The comparison describes two different responses; it does not measure the actual gap between salaries.
Purchasing power also provides a distinct indicator: 48,4% state that it has decreased. The source therefore juxtaposes satisfaction with remuneration and loss of purchasing power without attributing a causal relationship between the two data points. The survey captures perceptions reported by participants; it does not present individual pay slips or an average salary.
### Who conducted the research
The work stems from collaboration between BiblioLavoro, the Cisl branches of the Lakes, Sondrio and Eastern Piedmont, and OCST. The article presents it as a Cisl study on workers who cross the border daily. The location indicated for the presentation is Varese; the source does not provide a calendar date beyond the reference to Saturday.
This basis allows the figures to be read as results from the sample of 1.542 people. The text does not provide a breakdown by profession, company or individual territory. Therefore, the comparison among perceptions of pay, satisfaction and purchasing power remains as reported by the survey, without extending it to categories not described. The second segment of the survey highlights commuting times: for almost one third of the sample, the journey between home and work takes more than an hour and a half per day. A private car is used by 73,2% of respondents, while for almost half of the sample, mobility costs account for between 5 and 10% of their salary. The possibility of working remotely, which would help reduce travel, applies to only 37,4% of the sample.
Taken together, these figures compare time, expenditure, means of transport used, and the possibility of working remotely, but do not establish that one item causes the other. The gap between the 73,2% who use a car and the 37,4% who have access to remote working is 35,8 percentage points. This is a difference between two shares from the same survey, not a measure of how many motorists cannot work remotely: the source does not cross-reference individual responses.
### Comparison of the indicators
| Indicator | Survey result | |---|---| | Journey | Almost one third exceeding an hour and a half per day | | Means of transport | 73,2% using a private car | | Mobility | Almost one in two between 5 and 10% of their salary | | Remote working | Available to 37,4% |
The reference to 10% indicates the upper limit of the range reported by the study, not an average expense. The source also does not calculate an individual amount or distinguish between different distances or travel methods. The figure therefore makes it possible to measure the stated burden of mobility, not to reconstruct the cost incurred by each cross-border commuter.
The survey also finds a gender difference in terms of pay: 25,4% of female workers earn less than 3.000 gross francs per month, compared with 8,2% of men. The gap, calculated by subtracting the published percentages, is 17,2 percentage points. The source also specifies that men are more represented in the salary bracket above 5.000 francs, without providing the exact share.
This comparison also describes a distribution, but does not explain its reasons. The study does not indicate occupations, seniority, hours worked, or other factors useful for breaking down the gap. The available data therefore show differences between groups and commuting conditions, without turning them into a causal explanation. The survey also examines the possibility of moving across the border: only one in four respondents would be willing to do so in Switzerland. According to the wording of the study, therefore, the majority does not consider relocation an option. The high cost of living, the burden of health insurance premiums and the distance from family and loved ones discourage that choice.
This result should be kept separate from the other indicators concerning pay. The source reports the assessment of pay and willingness to relocate separately, without providing a cross-tabulation of the two responses. Likewise, it does not attribute the decrease in purchasing power to a specific cause. The survey therefore shows a stated choice and its main obstacles, but does not construct an individual profile of workers willing to relocate.
### The union's demand
In light of the results, Cisl is calling for a Statute for cross-border workers. Marco Contessa, the union's national head of Cross-Border Workers, argues that the specific circumstances of those who work across the border need to be recognized. The union identifies three priorities: a more predictable tax framework, pension transparency and a stable governance structure for cross-border relations. “A Statute is needed” is the wording with which Cisl summarizes the position presented.
Nor does it quantify an average salary, or specify the survey period; it only reports that the study was presented on Saturday in Varese. It does not break down the results by Canton Ticino, occupation, sector or individual company.
These omissions limit the interpretation: the figures show how the sample assesses pay, mobility, purchasing power and relocation, but they do not describe tax or social-security rules, differences between border crossings or routes, or trends over time. It is therefore not possible to turn these results into an individual estimate or a complete description of the conditions of every cross-border worker. Any further reading would require data that the source does not make available.

item.title: Cross-border healthcare workers: Como is gasping for air
item.description: Approximately 5,000 Italian border workers work in the Ticino health sector.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Around 5'000 Italian cross-border workers in Ticino's healthcare sector - Up to 12% in public hospitals - Up to 30% in the private sector - Health tax from 3% to 6% of net salary
## Key facts - People: about 5,000 Italian border workers - Scope: Ticino health - Peak in public hospitals: up to 12% of staff - Peak in the private sector: up to 30% of staff - Healthcare contribution: 3% to 6% of net salary
Approximately 5,000 Italian border workers work in the Ticino health sector. During peaks, their presence can reach 12% of public hospital staff and 30% of those in the private sector. The source indicates economic advantages as the dominant factor, but the cross-border appeal also depends on other reasons.
The service also gathers the motivations of two professionals. Federico Baldassarri, a nurse who has been working in a private facility in Lugano for a few months, explained that the main reason is the Swiss offer to a young graduate and the possibility of a considerably higher career development compared to the Italian context. Simona Franceschini, a colleague with a long career divided between the two countries, describes Switzerland as a leap in professional and human quality.
### The health tax doesn't stop the recall
The imminent application of the so-called health tax provides for a levy of between 3% and 6% of the net salary. The cost will be borne by border workers who were already working in Switzerland before July 2023, while the revenue will finance the Italian health service. According to the service, the measure does not seem to attenuate the cross-border appeal to Ticino health.
The news therefore concerns two distinct plans but connected by the workers: on the one hand, the numerical presence in the staff of Ticino hospitals; on the other hand, the professional and economic reasons that drive Italian personnel to work in Switzerland. The source does not present the tax as a measure already sufficient to change this choice and does not indicate other amounts, deadlines or application methods in addition to the share on the net salary and the reference to workers already active before July 2023. ## The comparison between public and private
| Area | Share indicated by the source | Time reference | |---|---:|---| | Public hospitals | up to 12% of staff | peak periods | | Private sector | up to 30% of staff | peak periods |
The first relationship discernible in the data is the difference between the two maximums: 30% minus 12% equals 18 percentage points. If 30 is divided by 12, the arithmetic ratio is 2,5. The calculation compares the maximum shares indicated for the private sector and public hospitals, but does not describe an annual average, an absolute number of workers per sector, or a trend over time. The source in fact uses the same framework of peak periods and does not provide any other intervals.
### Why working in Switzerland is attractive
The second comparison concerns the reasons for the choice. The economic advantage is identified as dominant; the testimonies, however, add two qualitative elements. Federico Baldassarri speaks of the offer made to a young graduate and of career development superior to that in the Italian context. Simona Franceschini, who has worked for a long time in both countries, instead highlights professional and human qualities. The source therefore does not reduce staff mobility to a single item on the payslip: it describes a combination of economic benefit, career prospects, and the quality of the career path.
The text does not report salary amounts, pay differences, or the number of hires. For this reason, it does not allow us to calculate how much more a healthcare cross-border worker earns, nor to estimate what share of the choice depends on each reason. The only quantified economic datum is the healthcare contribution ranging from 3% to 6% of net salary for the group indicated by the source.
The relationship with this measure is described in observable terms: the cross-border appeal does not seem to be dampened by the imminent application of the health tax. However, no before-and-after measurement is provided, nor a count of the workers who would have changed their decision. The data therefore documents the persistence of Switzerland's appeal according to the source, without turning it into a prediction about the future behavior of cross-border workers. ## The pressure on Como's hospitals
The difficulty concerns not only the ability of Ticino's healthcare system to attract personnel. According to the cited report, Como's hospitals are short of at least 500 staff members. The problem is presented as more widespread, because the shortage of medical personnel affects much of Northern Italy. The consequence indicated by the source directly affects patients: longer waits and greater difficulty accessing care.
Gianluigi Spata, president of the Como Medical Association, referred to the latest available data, concerning last year. In Italy, he stressed, 5,8 million patients gave up seeking treatment; the instances of foregoing care mentioned include examinations and follow-ups, associated with very long waiting lists. The figure concerns Italy and is not presented as specific to Como or Lombardy, so it cannot be equated with the shortage of 500 staff members in Como's hospitals.
### The union's assessment
Angelo Goffredi, a CISL trade unionist, commented on the comparison with the Swiss labor market. His assessment is unequivocal:
Angelo Goffredi, a CISL trade unionist, described competition with the Swiss labor market as unequal, comparing it to the challenge between David and Goliath, and observed that current measures do not allow for competition.
The statement attributes a trade-union assessment to the competition; the source does not add an action plan, new staffing figures or a measure of the difference between the two markets. Instead, the two sides of the phenomenon remain documented: Ticino covers part of its staffing needs with Italian personnel, and Como's hospitals face a shortage of staff.
The scope of the article is narrower than that of a general guide for cross-border workers. These aspects therefore cannot be inferred from the reported data. To relate the indicated share to net salary, tax calculator is available.
*Source: [rsi.ch](https://www.rsi.ch/s/4185242)*
Article 1(237–238) of Italian Law No. 213/2023 does not apply indiscriminately to all cross-border workers. It covers: (a) Italian residents who work and stay in Switzerland and use the Italian SSN; (b) frontier workers under Article 9(1) of the Italy–Switzerland Agreement whose income is taxable only in Switzerland and who exercised the legal right to choose health insurance; and (c) dependants of those two categories. Paragraph 238 sets a progressive 3–6% share of net Swiss salary, with a €30 minimum and an ordinary €200 maximum for each month worked from 2024. The cap may be doubled in cases of omitted payment or omitted communication specified in Article 1(100) of Law No. 207/2024. The Region of residence sets the rates and procedure each year.

item.title: Cross-border commuters questionnaire: salary okay but too much commuting
item.description: 1.542 online responses collected in May 2026 73% satisfied with their salary 31,7% spend more than an hour and a half traveling every day 76,9% would
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 1.542 online responses collected in May 2026 - 73% satisfied with the salary - 31,7% spend more than an hour and a half commuting every day - 76,9% would not move to Switzerland
## Key facts - Research → «Working across borders: conditions, needs and prospects of cross-border workers» - Responses → 1.542 workers - Period → May 2026 - Presentation → Saturday, October 24, at 9.30 - Location → Centro Congressi Ville Ponti di Varese - Promoters → CISL dei Laghi, CISL Sondrio, CISL Piemonte Orientale and OCST - Coordination → BiblioLavoro, study center of CISL Lombardia
Almost 32 thousand cross-border workers leave the province of Como every day to work in Switzerland and return in the evening, crossing the border again.
The promoters are CISL dei Laghi, CISL Sondrio, CISL Piemonte Orientale and the Ticino trade union OCST; scientific coordination was handled by BiblioLavoro, the study center of CISL Lombardia. In May 2026, the online questionnaire collected responses from 1.542 workers. The stated objective is to go beyond official statistics by giving cross-border workers a direct voice on how their work is changing, in order to turn this feedback into concrete proposals.
### Satisfactory salary, more complex picture
Salary prospects are among the main reasons for choosing Switzerland: 73% of respondents view their salary positively. But 48,4% state that their purchasing power has declined in recent years.
Moreover, 55,6% believe that, for the same duties, their remuneration is lower than that of a Swiss resident; among those not covered by a collective agreement, the share reaches 63,4%. In addition, 42,7% report having experienced at least once treatment they perceived as discriminatory because they were a cross-border worker. The questionnaire thus provides a picture that includes declared satisfaction, purchasing power, salary comparison and perception of discrimination, without reducing the experience to a single indicator. ## Employee benefits, commuting and teleworking
The responses collected show that the assessment of cross-border work does not depend solely on salary. Employee benefits receive a decidedly critical assessment: 58,9% of respondents are not satisfied with them. For the majority, contributions for transportation, meal vouchers or production bonuses are lacking. The research identifies these as concrete parts of the work experience, alongside salary.
### The cost of time
The questionnaire describes time as one of the least visible costs of cross-border work. 31,7% of workers spend more than an hour and a half a day commuting between home and work. 73,2% mainly use private cars. The source does not provide a breakdown of commuting times by province or border crossing: the available figure therefore concerns all respondents.
Teleworking introduces a separate comparison. Only 37,4% work for companies that allow it for cross-border workers, but among those who use it, 95,2% approve of it, almost unanimously.
| Indicator | Research result | |---|---:| | Companies that allow cross-border workers to telework | 37,4% | | Users who approve of it | 95,2% | | Remote workers satisfied with work-life balance | 69,5% | | Workers working exclusively on-site satisfied with work-life balance | 51,8% |
The comparison between the 69,5% of those who work remotely and the 51,8% of those who work exclusively on-site describes a difference in responses concerning work-life balance. However, on its own, it does not demonstrate a cause-and-effect relationship: the source presents percentages referring to different groups and not a forecast of the future effects of teleworking. ## Health, social security and life choices
### Issues that remain open
87.8% of respondents consider the so-called “health tax” penalizing. As for the second pillar, there is a strong need for information: 69.2% state that they have little or no knowledge of how their pension fund operates. This is a figure concerning the knowledge reported by respondents, not a technical assessment of individual pension positions.
The propensity to move to Switzerland is limited: 76.9% would not consider this possibility. The publication therefore regards cross-border employment as a stable life choice, not a step toward emigration.
In addition to the analysis, the publication devotes a second section to trade union proposals: extend collective bargaining in Switzerland; implement the Statute of Cross-Border Workers and the NASpI already provided for by Law 83/2023; raise the tax threshold for telework; strengthen the service network between OCST and CISL, including INAS and CAF.
The scope of the research remains precise. The second pillar is mentioned, but no technical data on the LPP or references to INPS are provided. These topics therefore cannot be presented as findings of the questionnaire: the source documents salaries, welfare, commuting, telework, health, social security and intentions to move.

It covers: (a) Italian residents who work and stay in Switzerland and use the Italian SSN; (b) frontier workers under Article 9(1) of the Italy–Switzerland Agreement whose income is taxable only in Switzerland and who exercised the legal right to choose health insurance; and (c) dependants of those two categories. Paragraph 238 sets a progressive 3–6% share of net Swiss salary, with a €30 minimum and an ordinary €200 maximum for each month worked from 2024. The cap may be doubled in cases of omitted payment or omitted communication specified in Article 1(100) of Law No. 207/2024. The Region of residence sets the rates and procedure each year.

item.title: 13th AVS payment: vote on VAT, possible rate of 8,5% from 2028
item.description: The standard VAT rate would increase from 8,1 to 8,5%.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The standard VAT rate would rise from 8,1 to 8,5%. - The increase is indicated as starting in 2028. - The vote referred to is set for November 29. - The 13th AVS pension payment is presented as awaiting funding.
## Key facts - Subject → financing of the 13th AVS - Starting rate → 8,1% - Assumed rate → 8,5% - Stated effective date → 2028 - Vote → November 29
### The issue identified by the source
The original source presents the 13th AVS as a measure still awaiting financing. The funding is linked to the possibility that the standard VAT rate will rise from 8,1 to 8,5% starting in 2028.
The wording is cautious and does not amount to an announcement of a decision that has already entered into force. The reference to “or not?” indicates that the outcome remains linked to the vote on November 29. The material does not indicate the year of the vote, nor does it specify the expected revenue, the amount of the 13th AVS, or the share of funding that would derive from VAT.
For those following Swiss affairs from across the border, the verifiable information is therefore limited: the discussion concerns financing the 13th AVS and a possible change to the standard rate. No names of sponsoring authorities, statements by political parties, or implementation details are reported. Nor is it indicated whether the change would affect other VAT rates.
The news, as provided, does not make it possible to turn the hypothesis into an individual cost. A calculation basis and an individual amount are missing. The key figure to retain is the comparison between 8,1% and 8,5%, with effect indicated from 2028, while the decision is linked to the vote on November 29. ## The comparison between the two values
The change indicated by the source is 0,4 percentage points: 8,5% minus 8,1%. It is an arithmetic comparison between two rates, not an estimate of a final amount. In fact, the text provides neither a typical expenditure nor a base to which to apply the change.
| Item | Reported data | |---|---| | Starting standard rate | 8,1% | | Hypothetical standard rate | 8,5% | | Arithmetic difference | 0,4 percentage points | | Indicated timing | starting in 2028 | | Political step referred to | vote on November 29 |
### The scope for cross-border workers
For a cross-border worker, distinguishing between the items is essential to avoid attributing effects to the news item that are not documented by the source. It does not quantify effects on withholding tax, tax rebates or double taxation, and it contains no specific data for the Canton of Ticino.
This limitation does not change the fact that the only social security scheme named in the text is the AVS. It does, however, prevent the funding of the 13th AVS pension payment from being confused with other social security and tax matters. The source does not quantify any effect for a worker residing across the border.
The only documented relationship therefore remains this: the funding of the 13th AVS pension payment is linked to a possible increase in the standard VAT rate. The numerical comparison can be made only on the basis of the figures presented. There is no basis for adding an individual calculation, a prediction about the vote or a definite consequence for the cross-border worker. ## The limits of the available information
The text provides a framework, not a complete implementation schedule. It says that the standard VAT rate should rise from 8,1 to 8,5% from 2028 and refers to the 29 November vote. It does not, however, indicate the full content of the question, the possible outcome, subsequent financing arrangements or the amount of the benefit. Without these elements, it is not possible to establish whether the increase will be approved or what the precise effect on spending would be.
### Separate the page references
The material provided also contains separate references to other news items. One reports the release of a Swiss citizen kidnapped in Niger on 13 April 2025; another indicates that, from 1 March 2027, the Federal Chancellery will have a new head. These two references are not presented as parts of the dossier on the 13th AVS and do not add data to its financing. Keeping them separate avoids attributing to the vote information that belongs to other headlines on the page.
The territorial scope also remains generic. The text of the news item does not mention municipalities in Ticino, border crossings, companies, affected workers or individual amounts. Therefore, it is not possible to construct a concrete case for someone who crosses the border or automatically link the hypothesis about VAT to withholding tax, LAMal or rebates.
The only documented conclusion is narrower: the financing of the 13th AVS is associated with a possible increase in the standard VAT rate, with effect indicated from 2028 and with the 29 November vote as a step mentioned in the text.
Anyone who wants to keep the pension topic separate from other calculations can consult AVS and LPP calculator, without using this article to infer amounts that the source does not provide.

item.title: Bellinzona inaugurates the first cycle path
item.description: Three kilometres mark Bellinzona's first official entry into the world of «cycle streets».
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Bellinzona inaugurates its first cycle street - The route is three kilometers long - The route runs from Giubiasco to Bellinzona - Bicycles and motorized traffic share the carriageway
## Key facts - Project → first cycle street in the City - Length → three kilometres - Start → via Golena in Giubiasco - Finish → intersection of via Chicherio and viale Franscini - Roads along the route → via Maestri Comacini and via Raggi - Purpose → connect the neighbourhoods and facilitate daily travel
### A route between Giubiasco and Bellinzona Three kilometres mark Bellinzona's first official entry into the world of «cycle streets». The City has inaugurated a cycle street that starts from via Golena, in Giubiasco, and reaches the intersection of via Chicherio and viale Franscini, in Bellinzona. The route also passes along via Maestri Comacini and via Raggi.
The project is not limited to opening a connection: on the roadway, bicycles and motor traffic share the space, according to a coexistence model that places safety and the quality of the cycling route at the centre. The trial therefore also concerns how different users make use of the same area.
The initiative is also a test bed for new cycling mobility solutions in Bellinzona. It also forms part of the City's efforts to consolidate the active mobility network and gradually improve connections between the neighbourhoods.
The new cycle street aims to connect Giubiasco and Bellinzona within the municipal territory and make the bicycle a choice for everyday journeys as well, not just for leisure. The destinations considered include schools, services and workplaces. The project is associated with these daily journeys. ### Intersections at the heart of the trial The most tangible part of the intervention concerns right-of-way rules. The change required modifications to several intersections that, on sections with a 30 km/h limit, had until then been governed by right-hand priority. According to the source, this arrangement often gives rise to misunderstandings and risky situations, especially on roads used by many cyclists and pedestrians.
The first change described is right at the starting point on via Golena, in Giubiasco. Two intersections now have a Stop sign for those arriving from the right. The change is presented as a solution for making the flow of bicycle traffic safer, by intervening directly at the point where the paths cross.
Heading toward Bellinzona, the text then points to the complicated intersection between via Golena and via della Rongia. Here, the change is not described as another Stop sign, but as much clearer and more binding right-of-way signage. Cyclists and pedestrians on via Golena always have priority.
The comparison between the two locations makes the content of the trial clear: in one case, the rule is made explicit through a Stop sign for those arriving from the right; in the other, the right-of-way signage along via Golena is reinforced. The source therefore documents two distinct interventions within the same connection, both concerning the management of intersections.
These changes are connected to the everyday function assigned to the cycle street. If the route is meant to facilitate travel to schools, services and workplaces, the City also intervenes at points where sharing the carriageway can create misunderstandings. However, the text presents the works as a trial and does not report subsequent data on use of the route. ### A piece in the active mobility network
The project is presented as part of a broader municipal plan, not as a standalone project. Within this framework, the City aims to strengthen the active mobility network and gradually make cycling connections between neighborhoods more effective. The section between Giubiasco and Bellinzona is therefore one element of this network, even though its route remains defined by specific roads and intersections.
The connection emphasized by the City also concerns the quality of public space. Under this approach, strengthening cycling mobility gives people more practical, functional and sustainable travel options. The project is therefore both a road-traffic intervention and a test of an alternative use of the roadway.
There is also a reference to the timeline of safety requests. The changes at the intersections come nearly ten years after the interpellation submitted in 2017 by Ronnie David, then a municipal councillor for the Greens. Through that interpellation, David called for measures to improve the safety of cyclists and pedestrians. The source notes the temporal connection, but does not claim that the interpellation alone caused the works described today.
The text does not provide the cost of the project, the expected or recorded number of cyclists, any change in travel times, or data on the effect of the new signage. Nor does it indicate any changes to motor traffic beyond coexistence on the roadway and interventions concerning right of way.
No changes on these issues can be inferred from this announcement.

item.title: Ticino industry: 15 collective layoffs in 18 months, -900 cross-border commuters
item.description: In the last 18 months, numerous collective layoffs in Ticino 15 collective layoffs followed over a year and a half Approximately 900 fewer
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - In the last 18 months, numerous collective redundancies in Ticino - 15 collective redundancies tracked over a year and a half - Around 900 fewer cross-border workers over two years - Satisfactory orders, but without guaranteed continuity
## Key facts - Layoff period → last eighteen months - Collective layoffs followed → 15 - Fewer cross-border workers → approximately 900 in two years - Director interviewed → Stefano Modenini - Academic partner mentioned → SUPSI
Over the last eighteen months, in Ticino, collective layoffs in the industrial sector have been numerous and have fueled concern about the future of the sector. The analysis, however, offers a less straightforward reading: the origin of the situation is probably to be found in management’s strategic choices rather than in economic conditions.
The account begins with the warnings circulating in recent months. The media buzz associated the industry’s difficulties with the announcement of US tariffs, the strength of the Swiss franc, the increase in energy and transport costs caused by wars. The text specifies that the tariffs actually affected a very limited proportion of Swiss companies. The factors mentioned in the interview with Stefano Modenini also include the automotive crisis and the interruption of some transport routes.
### Orders and layoffs: two signals together
Modenini, director of the Associazione industrie ticinesi, describes a situation that is less concerning today than it seemed at the beginning of the year. A large proportion of companies, he reports, have a satisfactory order book for the coming months. Stability, however, does not amount to a guarantee of continuity: the wording used in the interview brings the two elements together without erasing the uncertainties.
Over the last year and a half, Modenini has followed fifteen collective layoffs. Half were linked to the industrial sector, while the others concerned the services sector. The figure describes the events he followed and falls within the same time frame as the eighteen months mentioned at the beginning. The account of the layoffs, therefore, coexists with an order book that, for most companies, appears satisfactory in the short term.
The issue involves two parties: Modenini offers the employers’ perspective, while Daniele Duma, head of GF’s melting department in Novazzano, describes the reality of his own company from the workers’ side. The future of Ticino’s industry is therefore examined both through business decisions and through the experience gained in production departments. ## Strategy matters as much as economic conditions
The central point of the in-depth analysis is the distinction between what happens in the short term and the choices that guide a company for the following years. A collective redundancy, Modenini explains, does not necessarily depend on a cyclical or economic crisis. A company may decide to diversify production or give preference to other production sites. In both cases, the region is compared with other regions.
| Short-term signal | Strategic horizon | |---|---| | Satisfactory order book for the coming months | Future-oriented development plans | | Tariffs, franc, energy, transport and communication routes | Diversification or other production sites | | Stability without a guarantee of continuity | Attractiveness of the region compared with other regions |
The value of this comparison is to distinguish between two dimensions that may overlap in the public alarm. The order book gives a snapshot of the prospects for the coming months; decisions regarding production and sites, on the other hand, concern the following years. The source does not present the stability of orders as a guarantee of continuity, nor does it consider a collective redundancy automatic proof of a cyclical crisis.
### The region as an industrial parameter
The discussion of framework conditions makes the relationship between the company and the region concrete. Modenini cites legal stability, taxation, costs and the availability of labor. Improving these conditions, according to the interview, means reducing the risk that a company will leave the region. The assessment of attractiveness therefore concerns not only the immediate cost, but also the possibility of organizing operations in subsequent years.
The same reasoning applies to innovation. The Swiss industrial sector is recognized worldwide for its technical quality and innovative capacity, but introducing innovation requires investments in tools, training and process updates. The source describes companies at different stages: some still have to begin digitization, while others are integrating artificial intelligence.
As for public instruments, the Innovation Act provides funding, but the interview points to the need to do something different and to put in place targeted instruments for small and medium-sized enterprises. Collaboration with academic partners, such as SUPSI, is instead described as positive. The framework thus combines technical quality, vocational training, research and process updates: these are the elements that the source places alongside management's strategic choices. ## Labour and the border: the documented scope
The staff shortage links the issue of cross-border workers to the difficulties facing industry. The labour shortage is identified as one of the sector's main challenges and, especially in Ticino, the problem is exacerbated by the introduction of the tax agreement with neighbouring Italy that governs the taxation of cross-border workers. Modenini is also asked to consider the relationship with the demographic crisis and the agreement's possible deterrent effect on higher-income workers interested in employment in Ticino.
The reported response begins with a figure in the statistics on cross-border workers: over two years, approximately 900 female and male workers were lost, partly for age-related reasons. This passage is relevant to the canton of Ticino because it connects workforce availability with the issue of the region's attractiveness, already identified in the interview among the conditions companies assess when deciding how to organise production. The text therefore reports, in the same passage, the figure for the loss of approximately 900 female and male workers and the indication of age-related reasons.
### The date of the agreement and tax treatment
The New Agreement on Cross-Border Workers was signed on 23 December 2020 and has been in force since 1 January 2024; Italy's ratification is Law 83 of 13 June 2023. The same reference specifies that withholding tax on the employment income of cross-border workers is collected in Switzerland and that Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit in the CE section of Form 730.
These latter elements are part of the verified reference and should not be attributed to Modenini's statements. They serve to situate in time and in tax terms the agreement referred to by the industry source; the source instead presents it in relation to workforce availability in Ticino.
The passage remains focused on cross-border work and does not become a guide to the G permit, AVS, LPP, LAMal or tax rebates. The documented scope is industrial: collective redundancies, strategic choices, innovation, training, order book and staff availability. Administrative procedures or benefits not described are therefore not added. The picture of Ticino's industry emerges from the interplay between companies' decisions, the training required by innovation and the availability of female and male workers.

item.title: Arrest in Ticino in international anti-mafia operation
item.description: A person was arrested in Ticino on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
In brief - A person arrested in Ticino on Wednesday. - The operation led to 30 arrests. - False invoices discovered for over 110 million euros. - International money laundering of 68 million via cryptocurrencies.
Key facts - Location → Canton Ticino - Coordination → Milan DDA - Operation → Guardia di Finanza of Milan and Monza - Arrests → 30 - False invoices → over 110 million euros - Money laundering → 68 million euros via cryptocurrencies - Searches → Ticino, Spain and several Italian provinces - Deployment → over 350 Guardia di Finanza officers
### Arrest in Canton Ticino In the 12:30 radio newscast of October 21, 2026, the report signed by Alain Melchionda reports the arrest, which took place on Wednesday in Ticino, of a person involved in a large anti‑mafia operation by the Guardia di Finanza of Milan and Monza. The investigation was coordinated by the Milan District Anti‑Mafia Directorate (DDA).
The investigation dismantled the hidden bank of organized crime. The source indicates the involvement of members of the ’ndrangheta, the Camorra and the Fourth Mafia, i.e. the Foggia organized crime. The reported tally includes 30 arrests, over 110 million euros in false invoices and an international money‑laundering scheme of 68 million euros via cryptocurrencies.
For the part carried out in Switzerland, Fedpol conducted several house searches in Canton Ticino at the request of the Milan DDA and on behalf of the Federal Office of the Attorney General. The arrested person was placed in detention for extradition purposes.
Search activities continue in Spain and in several Italian provinces, involving over 350 Guardia di Finanza officers. The report thus describes an action extending beyond Ticino territory, without specifying which provinces are involved or linking the 30 arrests to specific locations. The Ticino municipality concerned and the identity of the person are also not indicated. ## Cooperation between the authorities The report distinguishes between the coordination of the investigation and the activities carried out in the Canton of Ticino. The Guardia di Finanza in Milan and Monza conducted the major anti-mafia operation, while the Milan District Anti-Mafia Directorate, referred to as the DDA, coordinated it. For the house searches in the Canton of Ticino, the source identifies Fedpol: the operations were carried out at the request of the Milan DDA and on behalf of the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland.
### The sequence indicated by the source In the report, the Ticino arrest is included in the same operation that involved multiple territories. In addition to the Canton of Ticino, searches are under way in Spain and in several Italian provinces. The source links the deployment of more than 350 Guardia di Finanza personnel to the activities described, but does not provide a breakdown of personnel by country, province, or individual search.
| Step | Entity or location | Information reported | | Coordination | Milan DDA | Coordinates the operation | | Conduct | Guardia di Finanza in Milan and Monza | Conducts the operation | | Ticino | Fedpol | Several house searches | | Assignment | Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland | Activities in Ticino | | Other locations | Spain and several Italian provinces | Searches under way | | Personnel | Guardia di Finanza | More than 350 personnel |
The cooperation described by the source therefore links the Italian activity to that carried out in the Canton of Ticino, without changing the roles indicated. The Milan DDA appears as the authority that coordinates and requests the operations; Fedpol conducts the house searches in Ticino on behalf of the Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland. The report does not indicate the Italian provinces involved, the Spanish locations, or the Ticino municipality concerned. Nor does it attribute the 30 arrests to individual territories. ## The investigation's figures and what is not indicated The financial aspect of the story is based on two distinct pieces of data. On the one hand, the investigation led to the discovery of over 110 million euros in false invoices; on the other, the source quantifies the international money laundering through cryptocurrencies at 68 million euros. The report does not provide an overall total and does not clarify whether the two amounts coincide. This article therefore retains two separate figures, referring to two different elements of the investigation.
The definition of shadow bank also remains the one used in the report to describe the organized crime system dismantled by the operation. The source does not explain how this system worked, does not describe the methods used for the false invoices, and does not explain the stages of the money laundering through cryptocurrencies. The stated economic value and the cited financial channel are available, but not a technical reconstruction of the operations.
### The phase documented so far Operationally, searches are still underway in Spain and in several Italian provinces, with over 350 Guardia di Finanza personnel deployed. For Canton Ticino, the documented fact is the arrest of one person during home searches and that person's detention for extradition purposes.
The source does not give the arrested person's name, the Ticino municipality concerned, the individual charges, or the outcome of the extradition proceedings. Nor does it attribute to that person a specific amount among the 110 million in false invoices and the 68 million in money laundering. Nor are subsequent developments after the searches underway described. The available reporting therefore stops at the results of the operation announced in the radio news bulletin of October 21, 2026, without adding local consequences or judicial decisions not reported.

item.title: Varese transport commitments: Vedano spur, Gallarate-Luino
item.description: The debate on the Regional Mobility and Transport Plan (PRMT), which lasted for more than a week in the Regional Council, led the PD and the other
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The Pd secures commitments regarding the PRMT in Lombardia - The Peduncolo di Vedano is included in further studies - Gallarate-Luino is included in the design phases of the Plan - Passenger use of the Luino-Sesto Calende line will be assessed
## Key facts - Plan: Regional Mobility and Transport Plan (PRMT) - Territory: province of Varese - Project: Vedano Olona spur road - Line: Gallarate-Luino - Assessment: passenger use of the Luino-Sesto Calende line - Status of the Luino-Sesto Calende line: currently reserved for freight
The debate on the Regional Mobility and Transport Plan (PRMT), which lasted for more than a week in the Regional Council, led the PD and the other opposition parties to secure commitments on public transport. For the province of Varese, the outcomes include two motions submitted by PD regional councillor Samuele Astuti: one devoted to the Vedano Olona spur road, the other to the Gallarate-Luino railway line and the possibility of opening the Luino-Sesto Calende line to passenger traffic.
### Spur road: further studies and timeline The first commitment calls on the Region to promote, in agreement with Anas, further design studies on the Vedano Olona spur road. The text also provides for a transparent assessment of the alternatives and the definition of a timeline.
The stated objective is to complete the project within the PRMT timeframe, but only if the further studies produce positive results. The commitment described therefore concerns the preparatory work, the comparison of alternatives and the indication of the timetable.
### Railways: Gallarate-Luino and Luino-Sesto The second motion calls for the subsequent design phases of the Gallarate-Luino line to be included in the Plan, reconciling the needs of passengers and freight traffic with those of the areas crossed by the line and providing for appropriate environmental mitigation measures.
The requests also include an assessment of the possibility of opening the Luino-Sesto Calende line to passenger transport—currently reserved for freight—with the aim of restoring the railway connection between the municipalities located on the western shore of Lake Maggiore. Astuti summarized the request: «Now what is needed are defined timelines and concrete steps». ## Two commitments, two levels The comparison of the two dossiers shows different operational requests, while remaining within PRMT planning. For the Peduncolo di Vedano Olona, the source describes a process consisting of further studies, an evaluation of alternatives, and a timeline. For the railways, however, the agenda item concerns the planning of the design phases and calls for a specific assessment of passenger service.
### The comparison between the dossiers
| Dossier | Commitment reported by the source | Condition or scope | |---|---|---| | Peduncolo di Vedano Olona | Further studies with Anas, alternatives and a timeline | Implementation during the PRMT period if the outcome is positive | | Gallarate-Luino | Inclusion of the subsequent design phases in the Plan | Passengers, freight, areas traversed and environmental mitigation | | Luino-Sesto Calende | Assessment of passenger use | Line currently reserved for freight |
The main difference concerns the level of the request. In the case of the Peduncolo, the ultimate goal of completing it is indicated, but remains dependent on the outcome of the further studies. In the case of Gallarate-Luino, the text calls for planning the subsequent phases and simultaneously considering passenger transport, freight traffic and the areas traversed. For Luino-Sesto Calende, however, the source refers to an assessment of passenger use, not to the already-decided launch of a service.
This distinction is relevant to those who depend on the connections, including cross-border workers mentioned by Astuti along with commuters. The text identifies works and lines for which answers are needed, but does not indicate the number of users affected, schedules, train frequency or alternative routes. Nor does it provide a completion date for the Peduncolo or a date for the activation of passenger service on the Luino-Sesto Calende line.
The source therefore allows programming and further-study commitments to be described, but not the works to be presented as already completed or the railway connection between the municipalities on the western shore of Lago Maggiore as already operational. ## The regional framework and open issues The discussion on the PRMT concerned not only the dossiers of the province of Varese. For regional public transport, the Pd and the other opposition forces also secured these commitments: free access to public transport services for under-14s throughout Lombardy, reductions for under-26s, an automatic procedure for granting compensation to Trenord subscribers in the event of significant service disruptions, and the possibility of using the Carta del docente to purchase travel tickets.
These measures have a regional scope, while Astuti's two motions concern works and connections in the Varese area. The source therefore keeps separate the measures intended for public transport in Lombardy and the requests concerning the Peduncolo, the Gallarate-Luino and the Luino-Sesto Calende.
### The point still open Astuti also identifies the upgrading of the Malnate-Laveno line among the issues still open, together with the further interventions needed to make connections more efficient for the benefit of commuters and cross-border workers. The regional councillor announces that he will continue to insist during the budget debate as well, asking that the province's needs not be left behind.
### The limitations of the available data The text does not indicate funding, dates for the start or completion of the works, train schedules, service frequencies or an already defined outcome for passenger use of the Luino-Sesto Calende. The timetable for the Peduncolo is also presented as an objective to be defined, not as a schedule already published.
The reference to the cross-border worker remains general: Astuti speaks of connections for commuters and cross-border workers, without indicating individual cases. Nor does it address LAMal, rebates or withholding tax. For a comparison with mobility services in Ticino: Ticino public transport

item.title: Hacker attack on PK Softech: 27.000 IPCT members at risk
item.description: In late September, a hacker attack hit PK Softech, the software provider for numerous Swiss pension funds.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR
- 27'000 IPCT members could be victims - Attack on PK Softech in late September - Data on several hundred people in an IPCT folder - IPCT is preparing a letter to policyholders
## Key facts
- What → hacker attack on supplier PK Softech - When → late September - IPCT population → 27'000 affiliated people - Data on the server → information on several hundred insured persons - Letter → 17'000 active members and 10'000 pensioners - Investigation → Office of the Attorney General of Switzerland - Group mentioned → Akira
### The attack and the Ticino population
In late September, a hacker attack hit PK Softech, the software provider for numerous Swiss pension funds. According to the information in the report, the company’s server contained a folder named IPCT that contained data on several hundred insured persons. IPCT is the Pension Institute of the Canton of Ticino.
The possible Ticino scope is broader than the identified folder: 27'000 people affiliated with IPCT could be victims of the attack. The figure therefore describes the potential group indicated by the source, not a list of people for whom data theft has already been confirmed. The source specifies, in fact, that the extent of the damage in Ticino is not yet known.
Daniele Rotanzi, director of IPCT, highlighted the diversity of its members: they include teachers, administrative employees, state councillors, police officers and judges, as well as nursing-home staff and social workers from associations. This is the professional description provided by the director; the report does not offer a breakdown by place of residence or cross-border commuter status.
> “For now, we do not know for certain whether data relating to our insured persons are present.”
Rotanzi’s statement clarifies the main limitation of the report. The figure of 27'000 concerns the members who could be involved; the figure of several hundred concerns the data present in the IPCT folder identified on the server. The source does not establish whether the two figures coincide, or whether all the information in the folder was taken. Meanwhile, IPCT has announced a letter to its members, probably in the following week, to inform them of what happened and the possible risks, including the use of personal information by third parties. ### The count of policyholders
The decision to write to all policyholders allows an internal numerical comparison within the same communication. IPCT indicates 17'000 active people and 10'000 pensioners; the sum is 27'000. The basis is therefore the breakdown of the group communicated after last Friday's meeting. The source does not present these values as a time series.
| Group cited by IPCT | Number | What it includes | |---|---:|---| | Active members | 17'000 | policyholders receiving the letter | | Pensioners | 10'000 | policyholders receiving the letter | | Total | 27'000 | total of the two groups |
The calculation does not prove that all members of the two groups have been affected. It only shows how the total number of members is distributed in the communication announced by the institution. This is also a useful distinction because the report simultaneously refers to a potential group of 27'000 people and a folder containing data on several hundred people: the first figure concerns membership in IPCT, the second the documentation found on the server.
For a cross-border worker working in Canton Ticino, however, the source does not support an interpretation based on personal status. It does not quantify cross-border workers and does not indicate how many members have a G permit; These terms refer to topics that the report does not measure. It is therefore not possible to derive from this episode a proportion of cross-border workers involved, nor to link the possible risk to a tax regime or a specific border crossing.
As previewed, the content of the letter is more precise from a communications standpoint: IPCT wants to inform policyholders of the possibility of a personal data leak and of the possible use of that data by third parties. The tone will be calm. Policyholders will be told that pensions and contributions are safe, along with a warning to pay attention to unusual emails or phone calls. The source thus separates the security of pensions and contributions from the possibility of improper use of personal information. ### The comparison with Publica and the judicial follow-up
The reference to the Confederation's Publica pension fund helps keep the different aspects of the case separate. For Publica, the report states that information was stolen and identifies a population of 100'000 people at risk, including federal councillors, agents and military personnel. For IPCT, by contrast, the text speaks of a possibility: there is still no information on the extent of the damage in Ticino, and there is no certainty that insured persons' data are involved. The 100'000 for Publica and the 27'000 for IPCT cannot therefore be added together: they refer to two different pension funds, even though the attack hit the same software provider.
According to Tages-Anzeiger, the hackers have allegedly already demanded payment of a ransom. The conditional remains necessary even with reference to the Akira group: the hackers might have access to various types of personal data, from first and last name to the AVS number, including address, telephone number, email, pension data and IBAN. The list describes categories of potentially exposed information, but does not confirm that every field is present in the IPCT file or that it was stolen from insured persons in Ticino.
On the judicial front, the Office of the Attorney General of the Confederation has opened an investigation. IPCT then filed a criminal complaint requesting to be recognized as a private prosecutor, with the stated aim of maximizing the information it might receive. This is the follow-up documented in the source; no outcome of the investigation is reported, nor is there any definitive finding regarding the IPCT data.
Even for cross-border workers, the verifiable fact is therefore not an already established individual loss. The report does not identify insured persons, quantify the proportion of members potentially involved, or say that the data in the file were stolen. Instead, the report documents the attack on PK Softech, the presence of the IPCT file, the communication planned for insured persons and the legal initiatives launched. The information gap concerns precisely the extent of the damage in Ticino, which remains to be clarified.
*Source: [ticinonews.ch](https://www.ticinonews.ch/ticino/hackeraggio-casse-pensioni-centinaia-di-ticinesi-a-rischio-445085)*

item.description: Up to 1,3 million users in Switzerland may have been affected by the Revolut outage. The British digital bank reported difficulties accessing some
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Issues with payments, deposits and currency exchange - Disruptions began shortly after 8:00 in Switzerland - Google indicates a gradual return of services - Revolut: customers' money and data are safe
## Key facts - Who → users of the Revolut digital bank in Switzerland - Services → payments, deposits and currency exchange - Start → Tuesday, shortly after 8:00 - Cause → outage at Google Cloud in London - Restoration → gradual, with completion expected approximately by the afternoon
Up to 1,3 million users in Switzerland may have been affected by the Revolut outage. The British digital bank reported difficulties accessing some services on the morning of Tuesday, October 20, 2026. The operations affected included payments, deposits and currency conversions.
The disruptions began shortly after 8:00 in Switzerland. The source also reports repercussions for the services of banks, companies and online platforms in Europe. For this reason, the incident is described as an outage extending beyond the relationship between Swiss users and Revolut alone, although no list of the entities affected is provided.
### The stated cause and the return of services
The stated cause is an outage at Google Cloud, whose European data center in London was affected by serious network disruptions. Google stated that the problem had been resolved and that services were gradually returning to operation.
Recovery is not yet complete: customers may still be unable to create new workloads, while restoration for existing ones is estimated, approximately, to be complete by the afternoon. The source does not provide a more precise time.
In a message issued on October 20, Revolut reassured customers: all users' money and data are safe. The company added that it had been working on a solution since the problem was identified that morning and apologized to the people affected for the disruption. The clearest way to understand the case is to separate the operational level from the technical one. For users in Switzerland, the source describes difficulties accessing specific functions; at the infrastructure level, it indicates network outages at Google Cloud's European data center in London. It does not describe a series of independent failures for each Revolut function.
### The comparison between the two levels
| Level | What the source documents | |---|---| | Services | Payments, deposits and currency exchange are among the affected functions | | Infrastructure | Google Cloud reports severe network outages in London | | Recovery | Services gradually return to operation; completion of existing workloads is indicated for the afternoon | | Security | Revolut states that customers' money and data are safe |
This distinction avoids confusing the technical solution communicated by Google with the immediate availability of each function to the user. In the text, in fact, the problem is declared resolved, but the return of services is gradual. There is also still a possibility of being unable to create new workloads, while for existing ones the indicated time frame is only approximate.
For cross-border commuters, the documentable connection remains limited: payments and currency exchange are among the services mentioned, but the source does not specify which currencies are involved. It does not say how many users are cross-border workers, does not distinguish Canton Ticino from the rest of Switzerland and does not report effects on salaries, transfers or other work-related operations. The article can therefore describe a service disruption for Swiss users, without turning it into a measure of the impact on cross-border commuters. Revolut's communication completes the picture, without quantifying the impact. In a post dated October 20, 2026, the company assured that all its customers' money and data were safe. It also stated that it had been working on a solution since the problem was identified and apologized. This is reassurance about the security of the money and data, not accompanied by details about the availability of individual features.
### The limitations of the available data
The figure of 1,3 million is presented as the maximum potential number of users in Switzerland who could be affected, not as a count of users who actually experienced a problem. The source does not indicate which European banks, companies, or platforms experienced disruptions, nor does it specify which currencies are included in the exchange service.
The timeline also remains indicative. Google refers to services gradually becoming operational again and places the complete restoration of existing workloads by the afternoon; no definitive time is provided for each Revolut feature. The source also does not report an overall duration for the outage.
It does not limit the news to the Canton of Ticino and does not link the service disruption to a payslip, an employment relationship, or an INPS procedure. The term cross-border worker can therefore refer only to a potential reader interested in payments or currency exchange, not to a group measured by the source.

item.description: Saturday, October 24, in Luino, Palazzo Verbania on Viale Dante Alighieri will host «Cross-Border Workers 2026: Rights, Protection and Tax Updates».
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Saturday, October 24, meeting at Palazzo Verbania - Three sessions on tax, health and social security - Reception from 9.30; proceedings at 10 - Free admission, limited places
## Key facts - Event → «Cross-Border Workers 2026: Rights, Protection and Tax Updates» - Location → Palazzo Verbania, Viale Dante Alighieri, Luino - Organization → S.I.L.P.A., Associazione Comunale di Luino - Moderator → Fabrizio Tanchis - Reservations → 375 5576244; silpaluino.va@gmail.com
Saturday, October 24, in Luino, Palazzo Verbania on Viale Dante Alighieri will host «Cross-Border Workers 2026: Rights, Protection and Tax Updates». The program will focus on three topics: tax changes for those who work in Switzerland, healthcare protections available to those who live in Italy, and the calculation of the pension accrued across the border.
The event is supported by Studio San Giovanni, Caf Lavoro e Fisco, Folino & Tanchis, Studio Bottoni and Mutua MBA. Participants will be welcomed from 9.30, while proceedings will begin at 10. The discussion will be moderated by accountant Fabrizio Tanchis, head of S.I.L.P.A. in Luino. Official greetings will be given by Luino mayor and member of parliament Andrea Pellicini and by the president of the Province of Varese, Marco Magrini.
### The program
Cross-border work is undergoing a period of transformation. Since 2024, the new tax agreement between Italy and Switzerland has been in effect, with different rules for those who were already employed across the border and for people hired after July 17, 2023. Two regimes therefore coexist, while questions remain about income tax returns, social security and healthcare.

## TL;DR - Agreement signed on 23 December 2020 - Effective January 1, 2024 - Labour tax withheld in Switzerland - The Article 9 transitional regime applies only to workers who meet the Agreement’s definition and worked in Graubünden, Ticino or Valais between 31 December 2018 and 17 July 2023; covered employment income is taxable exclusively in Switzerland. The ordinary regime applies in other cases, with Italian taxation and credit for Swiss tax where applicable. The €10,000 in Article 4 of Law 83/2023 is only the income limit referred to in Article 1(175) of Law 147/2013, not a general allowance. [FTA factsheet](https://www.estv.admin.ch/dam/it/sd-web/Zbr5Jb-40aYm/int-laender-it-faktenblatt-faqs-it.pdf) · [Agreement, Article 9](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/en) · [Normattiva, Article 4](https://www.normattiva.it/atto/caricaDettaglioAtto?atto.articolo.numero=4&atto.codiceRedazionale=23G00087&atto.dataPubblicazioneGazzetta=2023-06-30&bloccoAggiornamentoBreadCrumb=true&classica=true&dataVigenza=09%2F09%2F2026&generaTabId=true&tipoDettaglio=singolavigenza&title=lbl.dettaglioAtto).
## Key facts - New Frontier Agreement → 23 December 2020; in force 1 January 2024 - Italian Ratification → Law 83 of 13 June 2023 - Old cross-border workers remain taxed only in Switzerland ([Art. 9 of the 2020 Agreement](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/it)). - The Article 9 transitional regime applies only to workers who meet the Agreement’s definition and worked in Graubünden, Ticino or Valais between 31 December 2018 and 17 July 2023; covered employment income is taxable exclusively in Switzerland. The ordinary regime applies in other cases, with Italian taxation and credit for Swiss tax where applicable. The €10,000 in Article 4 of Law 83/2023 is only the income limit referred to in Article 1(175) of Law 147/2013, not a general allowance. [FTA factsheet](https://www.estv.admin.ch/dam/it/sd-web/Zbr5Jb-40aYm/int-laender-it-faktenblatt-faqs-it.pdf) · [Agreement, Article 9](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/en) · [Normattiva, Article 4](https://www.normattiva.it/atto/caricaDettaglioAtto?atto.articolo.numero=4&atto.codiceRedazionale=23G00087&atto.dataPubblicazioneGazzetta=2023-06-30&bloccoAggiornamentoBreadCrumb=true&classica=true&dataVigenza=09%2F09%2F2026&generaTabId=true&tipoDettaglio=singolavigenza&title=lbl.dettaglioAtto). - Withholding tax → withheld in Switzerland
The New Frontier Agreement was signed on 23 December 2020 and entered into force on 1 January 2024. For the border worker who works or intends to work as a store manager in the Canton of Ticino, the first data to be read in the paycheck is taxation: the income tax at source is withheld in Switzerland.
The Italian ratification took place with Law 83 of 13 June 2023. Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit indicated in the EC framework of 730. The rule therefore excludes the idea of a deduction on the same income in both countries: the withdrawal at source is Swiss, while the credit operates in the Italian declaration.
### The distinction introduced by the tax calendar
The decisive step for a frontier worker is not the name of the commercial role, but the date that determines membership in the indicated regimes. Those who were already frontiersmen before 17 July 2023 are considered old frontiersmen.
For new frontier workers, the excess indicated is €10,000. The two thresholds are not interchangeable: they describe different audiences and must be read together with the date of entry into the regime. The data does not change the job description as a store manager, but changes the tax reference with which the income is interpreted.
Within the framework of border workers, the G. LAMal permit also appears. It concerns health insurance and not income tax; G border workers are granted the right of option. The healthcare choice must therefore be read separately from the tax withholding. To interpret the salary in Ticino, the distinction between source tax, social contributions and health insurance is more useful than an indistinct sum of the items. The second level to be separated concerns the Swiss contributions. The available percentages do not describe a single item and do not all have the same basis. The table makes the data readable without turning it into an automatic estimate of a store manager's net worth.
### The Swiss voices to distinguish
| Voice | Reported value | Specify | |---|---:|---| | AVS/AI/IPG | 5.3% | employee contribution | | AD/AC | 1.1% | cap of CHF 148'200 | | LAINF | 0.7–1.5% | indicated interval | | BVG | 7–18% | age range, from 25 years |
AVS/AI/IPG is indicated at 5.3% for the employee. AD/AC is at 1.1%, with a limit of CHF 148'200. For LAINF the figure is a range, from 0.7% to 1.5%; LPP is instead linked to the age group, with a value reported between 7% and 18% starting from 25 years. This structure explains why an isolated percentage is not enough to describe the net result: the items have different functions and criteria.
### Comparison with IRPEF
The fiscal period changes the comparison with Italy. For 2024–2025 incomes, the reported income tax rates are 23%, 35%, and 43%. From 2026 the framework indicated by Law 199/2025, art. 1 c. 3, it is 23% up to €28,000, 33% from €28,001 to €50,000 and 43% over €50,000.
In the data reported, 2026 concerns Italian IRPEF rates, not the entry into force of the New Cross-border Workers Agreement. These Italian brackets are not automatically added to the Swiss withholding tax. The documented rule for the cross-border worker remains the withholding of tax at source in Switzerland, with the tax credit in the EC framework of 730 to avoid double taxation. The comparison must keep the period, country and type of withdrawal separate.
Tax rates, including withholding tax and federal or cantonal tax rates, are established by federal or cantonal laws. At the federal level the indicated administration is AFC/ESTV; the cantonal tax administrations operate for the cantonal part. The role of those who administer the rates should not be confused with that of social security or statistical bodies. The Double Taxation Convention between Italy and Switzerland was signed on 9 March 1976. The conventional reference is distinct from the New Frontier Agreement of 23 December 2020, which entered into force on 1 January 2024. The institutional perimeter is also defined: Switzerland is not a member of the EU or the EEA.
### LAMal and permit G
For a border crossing with a G permit, LAMal indicates health insurance. It is not a health tax and does not coincide with the tax at source. G border workers have the right of option; for adults, the deductibles reported range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500. The data is health, while the withholding on income is tax: the two items should not be read as a single charge.
The distinction is also useful in the face of an offer for a store manager in the Canton of Ticino. Remuneration, AVS/AI/IPG contributions, LPP, withholding tax and LAMal coverage belong to different plans. The contribution rates allow you to sort the payroll items, but do not fix the value of the salary or net for each border worker. The framework provided quantifies percentages, thresholds, and deductibles; it does not transform those data into a single pay band.
### The administrative perimeter
Tax rates at source and federal or cantonal rates are set by federal or cantonal laws. AFC/ESTV administers the federal level, while the cantonal tax administrations follow the cantonal part. This distinction avoids attributing tax matters to structures that, in the framework indicated, concern social security or statistics.
For the reader, the documented point is therefore the separation between tax, contributions and health insurance, not an indistinct sum. The LAMal option right concerns health coverage, while the EC framework credit concerns double taxation. For an orderly numerical reading of the entries, the tax calculator is the relevant link.
Article 1(237–238) of Italian Law No. 213/2023 does not apply indiscriminately to all cross-border workers. It covers: (a) Italian residents who work and stay in Switzerland and use the Italian SSN; (b) frontier workers under Article 9(1) of the Italy–Switzerland Agreement whose income is taxable only in Switzerland and who exercised the legal right to choose health insurance; and (c) dependants of those two categories. Paragraph 238 sets a progressive 3–6% share of net Swiss salary, with a €30 minimum and an ordinary €200 maximum for each month worked from 2024. The cap may be doubled in cases of omitted payment or omitted communication specified in Article 1(100) of Law No. 207/2024. The Region of residence sets the rates and procedure each year.

The €10,000 figure in Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 is only the income limit referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013; it is not a general allowance for new frontier workers. Sources: [ESTV factsheet (Italian)](https://www.estv.admin.ch/dam/it/sd-web/Zbr5Jb-40aYm/int-laender-it-faktenblatt-faqs-it.pdf) · [Agreement, Art. 9](https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/2023/410/en) · [Law No. 83/2023, Art. 4](https://www.normattiva.it/atto/caricaDettaglioAtto?atto.articolo.numero=4&atto.codiceRedazionale=23G00087&atto.dataPubblicazioneGazzetta=2023-06-30&bloccoAggiornamentoBreadCrumb=true&classica=true&dataVigenza=09%2F09%2F2026&generaTabId=true&tipoDettaglio=singolavigenza&title=lbl.dettaglioAtto).
## Key facts - Work → cross-border welder in Canton Ticino - Permit → G - Income tax → withheld in Switzerland - Old cross-border workers remain taxed only in Switzerland (Art. 9 of the 2020 Agreement). - Convention → March 9, 1976
The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement was signed on December 23, 2020, and has been in force since January 1, 2024. Italy ratified it through Law 83 of June 13, 2023. For a cross-border welder working in Canton Ticino, the central tax issue is withholding on employment income. The source states that tax at source is withheld in Switzerland. Italy avoids double taxation through the tax credit indicated in section CE of Form 730.
“Old frontier workers” qualify under Article 9 only if they met the tax requirements and worked in Graubünden, Ticino or Valais during the stated period; covered employment income is taxable exclusively in Switzerland. There is no general €7,500 allowance; the €10,000 figure in Article 4 of Law No. 83/2023 applies only to income referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013. Separating these steps avoids assigning to 2026 an effective date that the source places in 2024.
### The distinction between old and new cross-border workers
The regime changes depending on the category identified by the source. The €10,000 limit is not a general allowance: Article 4 of Italian Law No. 83/2023 applies it only to the income referred to in Article 1(175) of Law No. 147/2013.
Permit G forms part of the administrative framework to be considered for cross-border work. Switzerland is not a member of the European Union or the European Economic Area. Here, the tax framework is defined by the dates of the agreement, the tax-free thresholds and the withholding rule. ## Withholding tax and comparison between periods
Swiss withholding and Italian IRPEF belong to areas that the source keeps distinct. For the cross-border worker's employment income, the withholding is in Switzerland; the credit in section CE of the 730 is the Italian mechanism cited to avoid double taxation. The Italy-Switzerland Convention against double taxation was signed on March 9, 1976.
### Comparing the Italian brackets
The Italian figure changes depending on the period considered. For 2024–2025 income, the indicated rates are 23%, 35% and 43%. From 2026, the source reports 23% up to €28'000, 33% from €28'001 to €50'000 and 43% above €50'000. For 2026, the stated reference is Law 199/2025, Art. 1 para. 3. The change to the middle bracket does not justify turning these percentages into an estimate of the welder's net income: there is no individual income to which to apply them.
| Period | Indicated IRPEF bracket | |---|---| | 2024–2025 | 23% / 35% / 43% | | From 2026 | 23% up to €28'000; 33% from €28'001 to €50'000; 43% above €50'000 |

They are not set by UFAS, which concerns social security, nor by BFS, which collects statistical data.
For the cross-border worker in the Canton of Ticino, the correct comparison therefore involves three separate elements: classification as an old or new cross-border worker, tax period and type of levy. Automatically adding an Italian percentage to the Swiss one would produce an interpretation incompatible with the rule of a single withholding in Switzerland and the Italian tax credit. ## Swiss contributions, LAMal and limitations of the available data
The percentages indicated do not in themselves define a net salary. The source lists some Swiss rates and contributions: AVS/AI/IPG equal to 5.3% for the employee; AD/AC at 1.1%, with the cap of CHF 148'200; LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5%; LPP between 7% and 18% depending on age bracket, starting at age 25. Therefore, the most solid information remains the cross-border framework: G permit, withholding tax, deductibles under the new agreement, Swiss contributions and LAMal. | Time | Content | Stated focus | |---|---|---| | 10 | Presentation of the research | Conditions, needs and prospects of cross-border workers | | Following this | First round table | Impact of cross-border work on the local economy | | 11 | Second round table | Role of institutions in promoting cross-border work | | 12.30 | Conclusions | Mattia Pirulli, national secretary of Cisl |
